content.intro: Learn grouping rows with group by through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Grouping Rows With GROUP BY matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: Grouping Rows With GROUP BY
content_blocks.alt_text: Product rows are grouped by category and transformed into one summary row per category with count and total inventory.
content_blocks.caption: GROUP BY changes the output grain from one row per product to one row per category.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The practical goal of grouping rows with group by is to produce a result set whose meaning is clear. Confirm which rows enter the query, how values are transformed or combined, and whether NULLs, duplicates, ties, or one-to-many relationships change the output.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Grouping by one column, Grouping by multiple columns, Grouping by expressions, Grouping and selected columns. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Grouping by one column
items.text: Grouping by one column helps you summarize rows with aggregate functions, GROUP BY, HAVING, conditional aggregation, and advanced subtotal operations. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.text: Grouping by multiple columns helps you summarize rows with aggregate functions, GROUP BY, HAVING, conditional aggregation, and advanced subtotal operations. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Grouping by expressions
items.text: Grouping by expressions works best when inputs and outputs have deliberate types. Use explicit casts when intent is unclear, guard against overflow or truncation, and avoid converting typed values to display strings before calculations finish.

items.title: Grouping and selected columns
items.text: Grouping and selected columns helps break a larger query into a precise question. Check the subquery's row count and output columns, account for NULLs in membership tests, and compare the result with a simpler equivalent on a small dataset.

items.title: Grouping joined tables
items.text: Grouping joined tables determines how rows from related sources are matched. Write the join predicate explicitly and check whether multiple matches can multiply rows; use a LEFT JOIN when unmatched left-side records must remain visible.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT c.name AS category, COUNT(p.product_id) AS product_count,
       COALESCE(SUM(p.stock_quantity), 0) AS units_in_stock,
       ROUND(AVG(p.price), 2) AS average_price
FROM categories AS c
LEFT JOIN products AS p ON p.category_id = c.category_id
GROUP BY c.category_id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(p.product_id) >= 0
ORDER BY c.name;
content_blocks.expected_output: The report returns one row per category, including empty categories because of the LEFT JOIN. COUNT(product_id) ignores unmatched NULL product IDs.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
